1

Foundations of Generative AI & Prompting

Theory

The goal is not to memorise prompt tricks. It is to give AI enough context, direction and constraints to produce useful work — and to know when the output needs verification.

What Generative AI Actually Does

  • Generates responses from learned patterns rather than functioning like a conventional database.
  • Can reason, summarise, translate, draft and restructure — while still producing confident errors.
  • Different models have different strengths: reasoning, long documents, web-grounded research and multimodal work.

The CRAFT Framework

  • Context — the situation and relevant background
  • Role — the expertise or perspective required
  • Action — the task to perform
  • Format — the structure of the output
  • Tone — the appropriate style and register

Use CRAFT as a mental checklist. The final prompt can read naturally — it does not need to display the mnemonic.

Why This Matters Clinically

  • Good prompts reduce ambiguity and make outputs easier to inspect.
  • Structured requests make it easier to separate facts, assumptions, uncertainty and verification needs.
  • Treat every AI output as a first draft or decision-support artifact — not a finished, citable answer.
“Trust the workflow more than the fluency of the model.”

Demo Prompt — Same Task Across ChatGPT, Claude & Gemini

Run the same prompt in each tool, then compare accuracy, clarity and usability
I am preparing a 15-minute teaching segment for second-year MBBS students on sensitivity and specificity. Explain both concepts using a clearly labelled 2×2 diagnostic-test table and one worked example with hypothetical numbers. Then create three single-best-answer MCQs with answer keys and brief rationales. Keep the explanation concise, distinguish simplification from clinical fact, and list two points the faculty member should verify before teaching. Do not invent citations.
Deliverable: one reusable, well-specified prompt and a practical understanding of why each instruction matters.
2

Research, Evidence & Academic Publication

Theory

Move from “searching for papers” to a repeatable evidence workflow: refine the question, map the literature, verify claims, then write.

Medical Research Assistant

  • Turn a broad idea into PICO/PICOT or another appropriate research question.
  • Build search concepts, synonyms and inclusion/exclusion logic.
  • Map studies by design, population, outcomes and limitations.

Clinical Evidence Verifier

  • AI-generated reasoning is not evidence.
  • Verify claims against current guidelines, systematic reviews and primary studies.
  • Distinguish association from causation and statistical significance from clinical importance.

Writing Is the Last Step — Not the First

  • Evidence retrieval shapes the argument you can responsibly make.
  • Claude and ChatGPT can structure and polish prose; the author remains responsible for data, interpretation and citations.
  • NotebookLM is useful for source-grounded Q&A over the papers and documents you actually provide.
Evidence → synthesis → argument → manuscript. AI can accelerate each stage, but it cannot assume responsibility for the evidence.

Demo Prompt 1 — Deep Research (Gemini / ChatGPT)

Use with Deep Research; inspect the linked sources yourself
I am investigating whether [intervention] improves [outcome] in [population]. Use Deep Research to map current evidence from relevant guidelines, systematic reviews and key primary studies. Present a table with source title, year, study design, population, main result, limitation and direct source link. Separate established findings from uncertainty, note conflicting evidence, and identify the sources I should open first. Do not say a source supports a claim unless the source itself supports it.

Demo Prompt 2 — Source-Grounded Q&A (NotebookLM)

Run after uploading the selected papers or guidelines
Using only the sources in this notebook, compare the findings on [research question]. For each conclusion, point me to the source passage that supports it. Identify disagreements between sources, missing information and questions the supplied documents cannot answer. Do not fill gaps with outside knowledge. Then list the exact study details I should verify in the original papers before writing.

Demo Prompt 3 — Structured Abstract (Claude / ChatGPT)

Use only verified study details; no invented results
Using the verified study details below, draft a structured abstract of no more than 250 words with Background, Methods, Results and Conclusion headings. Use only the information provided. If a required detail is missing, insert [AUTHOR TO COMPLETE] rather than guessing. Preserve the study design and numerical results exactly, and finish with a short checklist of details the author must verify against the manuscript.

3

Teaching & Assessment Creation

Theory

Use AI to accelerate teaching preparation without outsourcing pedagogical judgement: start with the learning objective, then build the teaching artifact.

Faculty Teaching Assistant

  • Lecture planning and learning objectives.
  • Clinical examples, progressive cases and discussion questions.
  • Formative MCQs, viva questions, handouts and revision material.

Good Assessment Design

  • Start from the learning outcome, not the question.
  • Align difficulty with the intended cognitive level.
  • Distractors must be plausible and clinically defensible.

Where AI Helps — and Where It Doesn't

  • Fast at generating variety, first drafts and alternative cases.
  • Weak at knowing your exact curriculum, learner misconceptions and local assessment culture.
  • Every AI-generated teaching artifact needs a subject-expert calibration pass.
AI can be the fastest member of your teaching team — but you remain the faculty member, examiner and educator.

4

Clinical AI & Decision Support

Theory

The clinical section shifts from “ask AI for an answer” to “use AI to interrogate the information, challenge reasoning and verify important claims.”

Report→Interpret→Challenge→Verify→Clinician decides

Decision Support, Not Diagnosis

  • Use AI to structure thinking, not transfer responsibility.
  • Separate what the source explicitly says from inference.
  • Make uncertainty visible.

The Firm Data Rule

  • Use only synthetic/de-identified cases in this workshop.
  • Never enter names, MRNs, identifiable dates, images or other unnecessary identifiers into general-purpose AI tools.
  • Apply institutional policy to real-world deployment.

What AI Is Particularly Good At Here

  • Extracting and structuring report findings.
  • Generating differential considerations and “what am I missing?” questions.
  • Surfacing red flags and missing information.
  • Finding and checking evidence when research tools are available.
Trust the workflow more than the fluency of the model — a confident answer is not the same as a correct one.
4

Clinical Decision Support

Demo

Participants work through one synthetic clinical report and progressively interrogate it using reusable Claude Skills.

Skill Workflow

  • Report Interpreter → extract, explain, limit and correlate.
  • Differential Challenger → broaden and stress-test the working diagnosis.
  • Evidence Verifier → verify the important claims.
  • Reasoning Challenger → identify assumptions and what could falsify the interpretation.

Tools Demonstrated

ClaudeChatGPTGeminiPerplexityGlass Health

Demo Prompt 1 — Report Interpreter (Claude Skill)

Synthetic case only · separate report facts from interpretation
This is a synthetic, de-identified [X-ray / CT / ECG / pathology] report used for education. Act as a clinical report interpreter. First reproduce only the findings explicitly stated in the report. Then separate (1) what the report says, (2) what those findings may mean, (3) what cannot be concluded from this report alone, and (4) red flags or missing clinical context. Do not invent findings or make a definitive diagnosis. List the questions and source claims a clinician should verify independently. Keep uncertainty visible and leave the final interpretation to the clinician.
Capability upgrade · 5 minutes

Use the second model to challenge — not validate — the first

Claude Skills: Build Reusable Workflows

New

A Skill is a reusable set of instructions and resources that Claude follows for a repeatable job. The point is not to write the same complex prompt every time — it is to build a workflow you can reuse, test and improve.

🩻

Clinical Report Interpreter

Report → explicit findings → meaning → limitations → clinical correlation → red flags → verification.

Imaging · ECG · Pathology · Labs
🧠

Clinical Differential Challenger

Case → alternatives → contradictory evidence → dangerous possibilities → information gain.

Anti-anchoring
🔎

Clinical Evidence Verifier

Claim → current source → quality → relevance → limitations → verified conclusion.

Guidelines · Primary literature
🩺

Reasoning Challenger

Working diagnosis → assumptions → what doesn't fit → alternatives → what would falsify it.

Cognitive forcing
📚

Medical Research Assistant

Research idea → question → search strategy → evidence map → gap → study design.

Research workflow
🎓

Faculty Teaching Assistant

Learning objective → lecture → case → MCQs → handout → formative assessment.

Teaching workflow
💊

Prescription Review

Structure prescriptions, flag missing fields and identify medication combinations worth checking — never auto-approve, auto-correct or replace pharmacist/clinician sign-off.

Clinical administration
Key distinction

Skill = how the work is done · Artifact = what the user can use

Reusable instructions

Define sequence, output format, uncertainty rules, source requirements and safety checks.

Usable deliverable

Generate a checklist, report template, teaching aid or interactive review interface.

Test & improve

Run a synthetic test case, inspect failures and refine the workflow before any real-world use.

Rule baked into every clinical skill: separate what the source states from what is inferred, identify uncertainty, surface red flags, recommend evidence verification, protect patient privacy, and preserve the clinician's responsibility for the final decision.
4c

Skill Spotlight: Prescription Review

Demo

Apply the same workflow discipline to a common task: structure, flag, verify — never auto-approve.

What the Skill Can Help With

  • Structure free-text prescriptions into drug, dose, route, frequency and duration.
  • Flag incomplete entries and questions for review.
  • Identify potential drug-drug or drug-condition combinations worth checking.
  • Convert a verified prescription into a patient counselling note.

What It Must Never Do

  • Auto-approve, auto-correct or dispense a prescription.
  • Process unnecessary patient identifiers.
  • Present an interaction flag as a definitive contraindication.
ClaudeGemini

Demo Prompt — Prescription Review Skill (Claude; challenge with Gemini)

Reusable instructions · synthetic data only · human sign-off required
Use this as the instruction set for a reusable prescription-review Skill. Input: a synthetic, de-identified medication list with [drug, dose, route, frequency, duration] and only the clinical context needed for review. Structure the entries into a table; flag missing or ambiguous fields; and identify drug-drug or drug-condition combinations that warrant checking. For each possible interaction, state why it may matter and name a reliable reference or source that a clinician/pharmacist should consult; if you cannot verify it, say so. Separate supplied facts, possible concerns and items needing professional review. Never infer a missing dose, auto-correct, approve, or recommend dispensing. Finish with a clear review checklist, not a treatment decision.

5

Visual Content & Productivity

Theory

Principles of Visual Communication

  • One idea per slide or diagram.
  • Use diagrams for processes and pathways; tables for comparisons.
  • AI gets you to a first layout quickly — editing judgement remains yours.

Where This Saves Time

  • Turn a rough outline into a coherent teaching deck.
  • Convert mechanisms and pathways into diagrams.
  • Draft meeting notes, emails and routine summaries.

The Quality Check

  • Does the visual make the idea easier to understand?
  • Is there unnecessary information?
  • Can the audience understand the hierarchy in three seconds?
Use AI to get to the diagram faster. Then simplify it further yourself.

Ethics, Governance & Responsible AI Use

Every workflow practised today sits inside a governance framework. The goal is not to fear AI — it is to know where the clinician, faculty member and author must remain accountable.

DO

  • De-identify patient information before using general AI tools.
  • Verify AI-generated citations, clinical claims and medication information.
  • Check current journal, institutional and professional guidance where disclosure or authorship is relevant.
  • Treat AI as an assistant to clinical and academic judgement.

DON'T

  • Enter names, MRNs, identifiable dates or identifiable images into inappropriate public AI tools.
  • List an AI system as an author.
  • Accept an AI-generated diagnosis, MCQ or citation without independent checking.
  • Assume one policy applies everywhere — check the relevant institution, journal or regulator.

NMC guidance on AI-generated promotion

The NMC’s October 2026 ethical advertising guidance restricts AI-generated promotional campaigns for commercial interest. Do not use AI to create patient testimonials, fabricated clinical outcomes, endorsements or misleading promotional claims. Permitted AI-generated content must be appropriately marked; verify the current official guidance before publishing.

Check official NMC notices ↗

Demo Prompt — Build Your Weekly Workflow

Choose tools by task, then define verification and privacy safeguards
I am a busy [specialty] doctor who wants to use AI for these tasks: [teaching task], [research task] and [administrative task]. Based on the tools demonstrated today, build a realistic one-page weekly workflow. For each task, recommend one primary tool or feature and one optional alternative; specify the input, expected output, estimated time, verification step and privacy boundary. Include a small 30-day trial with a measurable success criterion. Do not recommend putting identifiable patient data into general-purpose tools, and keep final clinical decisions with the clinician.

AI Tools: Which Tool for Which Job?

There is no single “best” AI tool. Match the tool to the task, then verify the output at the level the task requires.

ToolStrengthsWeaknesses / Watch-outsBest Use Cases
ChatGPTProjects for persistent task context; Deep Research for cited multi-source reports; file/data analysis and image generation where available.Features and usage limits vary by plan; citations and outputs still require inspection.Ongoing teaching/research projects, evidence reports, file analysis, visual explanations.
ClaudeSkills for repeatable instructions; Artifacts for editable docs, slides, designs and interactive tools.Templates and connected-app capabilities vary by plan/workspace; outputs still require review.Reusable clinical/admin workflows, teaching aids, checklists, interactive prototypes.
PerplexitySearch-first workflow with cited web sources; useful for current information discovery.Citations still need inspection; search summaries can inherit source-quality problems.Current guidelines, rapid evidence discovery, research scouting.
ConsensusResearch-focused evidence synthesis around published studies and scientific questions.Not a substitute for reading the primary paper; coverage and interpretation vary by question.Evidence questions, literature discovery, research background.
NotebookLMSource-grounded Q&A over documents the user supplies; useful for working from a defined evidence set.Answers are constrained by supplied sources and still need checking; not a universal evidence search engine.Guidelines, papers, teaching packs, source-grounded Q&A.
SciSpaceDesigned for reading and interrogating academic papers with structured assistance.Extraction/summaries can oversimplify nuanced methods or results.Paper reading, methods/results comprehension, literature triage.
Glass HealthClinical decision-support orientation with structured differential/clinical reasoning workflows.High-stakes clinical output requires clinician judgement, verification and appropriate deployment controls.Synthetic clinical vignettes, differential brainstorming, reasoning support.
GammaFast creation of polished presentation structures and visual layouts.Can prioritise presentation quality over scientific/teaching accuracy; review every slide.Lecture outlines, presentation drafts, visual storytelling.
GeminiDeep Research can use web, uploaded files and supported connected sources; Canvas can create/edit docs, apps, slides and quizzes.Source connections and advanced limits vary by account; generated claims and visuals require verification.Research discovery, research-to-creation, editable learning resources, quizzes and prototypes.
QwenUseful general-purpose alternative for comparison, multilingual work and broad task experimentation.Capabilities and performance can vary by model/version and deployment; less specialised for the workshop’s clinical workflows.Model comparison, multilingual drafting, general AI experimentation.
GeneralistResearchSource-groundedClinical reasoningVisuals
Use this as a task-selection guide, not a performance ranking. Features, model behaviour and access can change by version or plan. For clinical use, independently verify high-stakes claims and preserve clinician responsibility.
